catalog_quote: Matses has an alternating stress system where either all odd or all even syllables (counting left to right) in a (phonological) word are stressed (for phonetic characterization of stress see §2.7.1). The even- vs. odd-stressed pattern is lexically determined on all roots (this lexical stress can be shifted by some morphophonological processes; §2.6.5). Words composed of identical segment sequences can contrast with respect to being odd-stressed (110-115, a examples) vs. even stressed (110-115, b examples) ... (112) a. [tʃú.wa] 'heat up' b. [tʃu.wá] 'miss' ... I have found few minimal pairs, but there are contrasting monomorphemic minimal pairs (110 & 112) ... even-stressed roots and words are roughly three or four times more common than odd-stressed words. [p. 183] The stress system is quantity insensitive (i.e., not sensitive to syllable weight), but unstressed heavier syllables (i.e., closed syllables, especially those containing vowel sequences) often sound somewhat more stressed than lighter syllables. ... In any particular word, either all odd or all even syllables in the word are stressed. [p. 185] The rightmost word-level stress seems to be the strongest, but not very noticeably so (especially with words with varying syllable types), so I do not distinguish between primary and secondary word-level stress.

The even- vs. odd-stressed pattern is lexically determined on all roots (this lexical stress can be shifted by some morphophonological processes; §2.6.5). new_statements.rule_in_words: Binary alternating (every-other-syllable), quantity-insensitive stress across the phonological word; each root is lexically specified as odd-stressed (1st, 3rd, 5th.. = trochaic from the left) or even-stressed (2nd, 4th, 6th.. = iambic from the left), with even-stressed the default/majority pattern (3-4x more common, also imposed on loans and lexicalized forms); once the status of the first syllable is known, all other stresses follow regardless of suffixes. Phonetic correlates: vowel length and pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: All alternate syllables are stressed; 'The rightmost word-level stress seems to be the strongest, but not very noticeably so.. so I do not distinguish between primary and secondary word-level stress' (p. 185).
new_statements.exceptions: Prefixation shifts the stress of even-stressed roots but not odd-stressed ones (stress contrast can be neutralized, §2.6.5 pp. 165-168); monosyllabic roots are intrinsically stressed or unstressed, revealed under suffixation (tad 'plane' vs tsad 'sit', p. 185); verbs ending in /ke/ or /ka/ never stress that syllable and always stress the preceding one (p. 186); reduplicated forms and onomatopoeic animal names with reduplicated parts form two phonological words and do not follow the alternation (pp. 186-187, §2.8); Spanish loans often adapted to even-stressed pattern (§2.10). Footnote 37 p. 183: closely related Chiankuëshbo shows the opposite preference (odd-stressed more common).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (root + suffixes/enclitics; alternation does not carry across words in a phrase, p. 187). Separately, utterance-level stress falls on the last syllable of the utterance regardless of word stress and can mask word stress in citation forms; Fleck elicited words in non-final position (p. 182, 187).
new_statements.identity_note: Fleck 2003 describes Matses as spoken by the Peruvian Matses communities (Gálvez/Yaquerana rivers, e.g. Nuevo San Juan), i.e. mats1244 proper; his footnote 37 (p. 183) contrasts it with Chiankuëshbo (a closely related Mayoruna variety spoken by a captive woman), which prefers odd-stressed roots. Dorigo de Carvalho's work concerns Brazilian (Javari) Matsés of the same language.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the same text as the existing statement (Fleck 2003; the 2004 'UMI' entry is the microfilm/print issue of the Rice dissertation, dateAccepted 2003, and the MPI PuRe record links to the Rice repository whose PDF is byte-identical to the copy consulted). The catalog record for Matses has an empty rule field; Fleck supplies the rule: lexically assigned alternating (binary) stress, quantity-insensitive, no primary/secondary distinction, plus a non-contrastive utterance-final stress. Reading confirmed 'lexical (unpredictable)' with the refinement that the unpredictability is only the odd/even choice on the root; everything after it is rhythmic.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every other syllable of the phonological word is stressed, counting from the left; whether the odd or the even syllables carry it is a lexical property of the root (not predictable from segments or weight), so segmentally identical words contrast, e.g. [tʃú.wa] 'heat up' vs [tʃu.wá] 'miss'. Even-stressed (2nd, 4th..) words are three or four times more common than odd-stressed (1st, 3rd..) ones, so even-stressing is the default. Once the first syllable's status is known, the rest of the word, whatever suffixes follow, is predictable. Quantity-insensitive; phonetic correlates are vowel length and pitch. Separately, the last syllable of every utterance carries a non-contrastive utterance-level stress (§2.7.2) that can mask word-level stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 185: "The rightmost word-level stress seems to be the strongest, but not very noticeably so.., so I do not distinguish between primary and secondary word-level stress." Utterance-final stress is stronger than any word-level stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift under prefixation and (for monosyllabic roots) suffixation/encliticization, which can neutralise the contrast (§2.6.5, pp. 165-168); verbs ending in /ke/ or /ka/ never stress that syllable and stress the one before it (p. 186); some four-syllable CV roots take the default even pattern; reduplicated forms and onomatopoeic animal names fall outside the alternation (§2.8); bird-call imitations and some Spanish loans are re-stressed to the even pattern (p. 184); monosyllabic roots are intrinsically stressed or unstressed (p. 185). Footnote 37, p. 183: the closely related Chiankuëshbo variety shows the opposite preference (odd-stressed words more common).
new_statements.identity_note: Fleck 2003/2004 describes Matses as spoken at Nuevo San Juan and other Peruvian and Brazilian Matses communities (the language also called Mayoruna). Footnote 37 (p. 183) contrasts Chiankuëshbo, a closely related variety spoken by one captive woman living with the Matses, whose cognates are preferentially odd-stressed where Matses is even-stressed. The two SIL works use the older name 'mayoruna' for the same language (ISO mcf).

Aunque no se han encontrado pares con contrastes mínimos, hay contrastes entre palabras del mismo patrón silábico: /níni/ 'hija lejana' /nisí/ 'víbora' [...] En muchos casos la posición del acento se cambia con la adición de otros morfemas. (p. 23) [...] Se nota que aparentemente las diferentes combinaciones de tipos de sílabas no rigen la posición del acento. La regla general es que el acento recae en sílabas pares, empezando con la última sílaba de la raíz que es la segunda sílaba en la mayoría de las palabras. Pero recae también en sílabas impares. new_statements.translation: It appears that the position of the intensity accent (stress) is contrastive. Although no minimal pairs have been found, there are contrasts between words of the same syllable pattern: /níni/ 'distant daughter' /nisí/ 'snake' [...] In many cases the position of the stress changes with the addition of other morphemes. (p. 23) [...] Apparently the different combinations of syllable types do not govern the position of the stress. The general rule is that the stress falls on even syllables, starting with the last syllable of the root, which is the second syllable in most words. But it also falls on odd syllables. (p. 25)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress ('acento de intensidad') position is contrastive: same-shape words differ (níni vs nisí, séka vs sokó, čúmbo vs čombó, ónke vs akté). Syllable type (weight) does not govern placement. Default pattern: stress on even-numbered syllables counted from the word start, anchored on the root-final syllable (= 2nd syllable in most words) and alternating rightward (e.g. a.nó.sud.té, ba.tá.de.kít, ka.pís.kun.té), but odd-syllable patterns also occur (i.sí.to.dó, ón.ke, páis.čo.kít); adding morphemes can shift stress. Within a syllable, a two-vowel sequence stresses the second vowel unless /a/ is first (then /a/); in three-vowel sequences the last vowel, but /a/ always takes it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary ranking is drawn; the §4.2 pattern lists mark an accent on every other syllable of 3-5-syllable words (alternating rhythm, e.g. CV.CV́.CV.CV́C ba.tá.de.kít, V.CV́CV.CV́ i.sí.to.dó). §4.3 (p. 30) adds a separate phrase-level accent: 'un acento muy intenso.. mucho mas intensivo que el acento contrastivo (véase sección 4.1.), en la última sílaba de cualquier enunciación incluyendo a palabras en enunciaciones de una sola palabra' (a very intense accent, with length or laryngealization, on the last syllable of any utterance, including one-word utterances); rhythm groups noted but 'todavía no está analizado'.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress never falls on the suffixes /-ka/ 'transitivizador' and /-ke/ 'reflexivo' (únkaté, ónke, síkait); stress shifts when morphemes are added (pa.ís 'cuerno' vs páis.čo.kít); vowel-sequence rule has 'algunas excepciones.. que quizás se pueda explicar por reglas morfofonémicas'; across syllable boundaries stress may fall on any vowel of a sequence. Authors call the analysis preliminary (whole words, morpheme-structure rules not yet analysed).
new_statements.identity_note: Both ILV works describe the speech of the Matses ('mayoruna', self-denomination matsés) community of Yaquerana, prov. Maynas/Requena, Loreto, Peru (fieldwork Fields & Kneeland from 1969; Fields' 1970 analysis written up by Wise in 1974). Fields & Wise note dialect mixture in the community from captured women of other Panoan groups and say the study is limited as far as possible to the Matses system proper; DT14 notes speaker variation in o/u. Same language as Fleck 2003 (Matses of Peru); no separate dialect claim.

tone.quote: No Matsés, todos os dados observados no experimento mostraram a realização fonética da nasal em coda — não só no ambiente de pausa, como também em situação medial de palavra. A surpresa, no caso do Matsés, foi o fato de a nasal em coda assimilar ponto de articulação apenas nos casos de contiguidade às oclusivas labiais. Diante de todos os outros segmentos consonantais da língua, a nasal se realizou foneticamente como [coranal] — incluindo-se aí o ambiente de pausa. [...] a nasal subespecificada /N/ para o Marubo e a nasal coronal /n/ para o Matsés.
tone.locator: §4 'Considerações finais', journal pp. 190-191 (section heading on p. 190, quoted passage and the /N/ vs /n/ sentence on p. 191) (holds pp. 188-189)
tone.translation: In Matsés, all the data observed in the experiment showed the phonetic realisation of the coda nasal, not only before pause but also word-medially. The surprise, in the case of Matsés, was that the coda nasal assimilates place of articulation only when adjacent to labial stops. Before all other consonantal segments of the language the nasal was realised phonetically as [coronal], including before pause. [...] the underspecified nasal /N/ for Marubo and the coronal nasal /n/ for Matsés.
